introduction: On the ninth of July 1850 the Báb was suspended with a young disciple against a barracks wall in Tabriz and shot by a regiment. The guide gathers the telling of it, the grief of its anniversary, and the argument made from it for sixty years afterward: you thought this would end the Cause, and it spread. A Christian reader will hear the Passion throughout, and the companions make that hearing explicit: the reluctant official who washes his hands, the fellow-sufferer promised paradise, the silence of the lamb, “Father, forgive them”, the friends who had trusted “that it had been he”, the seed that must die, the lifting up that draws. Gamaliel and Joseph say what the persecutors could not foresee. Two voices keep the reader honest: the martyrs under the altar who cry “How long?”, and Wilfred Owen, who knew what the praise of dying can be used for.
questions: Pilate washed his hands, and Sam Khan sought to be excused. What do the readings make of the unwilling instruments of a martyrdom?
“We trusted that it had been he.” Readings 20 to 22 record the same collapse of hope. What turned it, in each story?
“Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die.” Is the growth of a cause after its founder’s death evidence of its truth? What would Gamaliel say, and what would a sceptic?
The souls under the altar cry for judgment; the readings move from grief to service and fellowship. Where has the demand for justice gone?
Owen calls the glory of dying for a cause “the old Lie”. What distinguishes remembering a martyr from recruiting by one?

outside.why: The anniversary is kept in grief. Is it nothing to you, all ye that pass by? behold, and see if there be any sorrow like unto my sorrow.
Persecuted in each city he came to. O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee.
The colonel of the Christian regiment did not want the task. Pilate took water, and washed his hands before the multitude, saying, I am innocent of the blood of this just person.
Pilate’s wife sent to him: have thou nothing to do with that just man.
A young man chose to die with him, and died at the first volley. To the one crucified beside him Jesus says: to day shalt thou be with me in paradise.
The disciple would not be parted. Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go.
Suspended in the square. He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter.
“God’s Love it was that sustained the Bab.” Love is strong as death; many waters cannot quench love.
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
Of what he thought, hanging on that wall. Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.
Would a life spent on worldly affairs have been better? Whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it.
The king slew him to extinguish the light. The light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not.
Martyred with those who were with him. They loved not their lives unto the death.
Tabriz, the place of martyrdom, is fragrant. England’s pilgrims rode to a place of martyrdom too, the holy blissful martyr for to seek.
An official wrote: this movement has ended. The two on the road to Emmaus had concluded the same: we trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel.
The friends were disheartened and the enemies rejoiced. Ye shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice: and ye shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy.
“You thought that if you martyred the Exalted One … this foundation would collapse.” Gamaliel: if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it.
The martyrdom strengthened the Cause a thousandfold. Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.
The lamp was expected to die out and its light spread. After Stephen’s death they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
Joseph to his brothers: ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to save much people alive.
“After the ascension of the Point, We raised up the Cause.” After Herod’s persecution: but the word of God grew and multiplied.
Sixty years after his death the remains were laid to rest on Carmel. Jacob in Egypt charges his sons: bury me with my fathers.
Many hastened to the arena after him. They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were slain with the sword: of whom the world was not worthy.

John sees under the altar the souls of them that were slain, crying: how long, O Lord, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood? The readings turn grief into service and fellowship. What do they do with this cry?
The ungodly “called Him a sorcerer”. Many said of Jesus: he hath a devil, and is mad; why hear ye him? Others said, these are not the words of him that hath a devil.
He was “the quintessence of meekness”. Learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart.
The martyrdom “raised his banner”. And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me.
Wilfred Owen warned against telling the young, with high zest, of the glory of dying for a cause. These readings praise a death. What keeps their praise from being what he condemned?

shortfall: Several readings repeat one image (the breast made a target for a thousand bullets) or one argument (the martyrdom did not end the Cause); they share companions.
